title: States of Matter and the Kinetic Molecular Theory

standard_code: Grade 10 Physical Sciences: States of matter and the kinetic molecular theory
standard_text: The three states of matter; melting point, boiling point and heating and cooling curves; the kinetic molecular theory: matter is made of particles in constant motion with forces between them. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 10, Chemistry: States of matter and the kinetic molecular theory)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): solids, liquids and gases, heating and cooling curves, melting and boiling points and the kinetic molecular theory. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid they move past each other; in a gas they move freely and far apart. Heating gives the particles more kinetic energy.

On a heating curve the temperature stays constant while a substance melts or boils: the energy is used to overcome the forces between the particles. The melting point and boiling point can identify a pure substance.

Example

Why does the temperature stay the same while ice melts?

Energy breaks the forces between molecules.

Answer: the energy is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to raise the kinetic energy

Example

In which state are the forces between particles weakest?

Particles are far apart.

Answer: gas

Common mistakes

  • Thinking particles stop moving in a solid.
  • Thinking temperature rises while water boils.
  • Mixing up evaporation and boiling.

faq.q: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?
faq.a: Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

faq.q: Why does a gas fill its container?
faq.a: Its particles move quickly in all directions and the forces between them are very weak.

items.q: What does the temperature of a substance measure?
c: the average kinetic energy of its particles
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: Calculate the mean kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 293 K.
More air is pumped into a car tyre (volume and temperature stay the same). What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: More particles hit the walls each second.

items.q: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of helium molecules (molar mass 0,00400 kg/mol) at 200 K.
items.e: ½m crms² = (3/2)kT, crms = √(3kT/m) = 1 120 m·s⁻¹.

items.q: A sealed syringe of air is put in a fridge. Why does the pressure decrease?
c: The mass of each particle changes.
The particles hit each other more often, not the walls.
The particles move more slowly, so they hit the walls less often and with less force.
items.e: Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls of the container.

items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

sets.title: Particles in solids, liquids and gases

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “Particles move randomly at high speeds in all directions.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “It can be compressed easily because there is a lot of space between particles.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
c: spread out in a regular pattern
closely packed in a regular pattern
closely packed in a random arrangement
far apart in a random arrangement
items.e: In a solid the particles are closely packed in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions, with very strong forces of attraction.

items.q: Which observation is evidence that particles move?
c: diffusion of a smell through a room
items.e: Particles spread from high to low concentration.

items.q: How do the particles move in a gas?
items.e: In a gas the particles are far apart in a random arrangement, moving randomly at high speed, with negligible forces of attraction.

items.q: What happens to the particles of a solid when it is heated (but does not melt)?
c: They vibrate more vigorously about their fixed positions.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a gas?
c: spread out in a regular pattern
closely packed in a random arrangement
far apart in a random arrangement
closely packed in a regular pattern
items.e: In a gas the particles are far apart in a random arrangement, moving randomly at high speed, with negligible forces of attraction.

items.q: Why do smoke particles move more quickly when the air is warmer?
c: The air particles move faster and hit them harder.
items.e: Temperature raises kinetic energy.

items.q: In a smoke cell, what causes the smoke particles to move randomly?
c: They are heated by the light.
They are hit unevenly by fast-moving, invisible air particles.
items.e: The air particles are too small to see.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “It has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: How do the particles move in a solid?
items.e: In a solid the particles are closely packed in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions, with very strong forces of attraction.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “Particles are far apart in a random arrangement.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “The forces of attraction between particles are negligible.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a liquid?
c: spread out in a regular pattern
far apart in a random arrangement
closely packed in a random arrangement
closely packed in a regular pattern
items.e: In a liquid the particles are closely packed in a random arrangement, sliding past one another, with strong forces of attraction, but weaker than in a solid.

items.q: Why are the moving air particles in Brownian motion not seen?
c: They are far too small to see with a microscope.
items.e: Only the larger smoke particles are visible.

items.q: What are the forces between the particles in a liquid like?
c: no forces at all, even when touching
strong forces of attraction, but weaker than in a solid
items.e: In a liquid the particles are closely packed in a random arrangement, sliding past one another, with strong forces of attraction, but weaker than in a solid.

items.q: What are the forces between the particles in a gas like?
c: strong forces of attraction, but weaker than in a solid
no forces at all, even when touching
items.e: In a gas the particles are far apart in a random arrangement, moving randomly at high speed, with negligible forces of attraction.

items.q: Why is a gas easy to compress?
c: There are large spaces between its particles.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: What causes the pressure of a gas in a container?
c: particles colliding with the walls of the container
items.e: Each collision exerts a force on the wall.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “It has a fixed shape and a fixed volume.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: What is internal energy?
c: the energy needed to melt a substance
the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles
only the kinetic energy of the particles
items.e: Melting increases potential energy at constant temperature.

items.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 0,800 kg of oil (c = 2 000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 5 K?
items.e: Q = mcΔθ = 8 000 J.

items.q: Why does the temperature stay constant while ice is melting?
c: the energy supplied breaks bonds (increases potential energy) rather than speeding up particles
items.e: This energy is the latent heat of fusion.

items.q: Why is a dull black surface best for a solar hot water panel?
c: it is a good absorber of radiation
items.e: Shiny surfaces reflect radiation.

items.q: What is absolute zero?
c: the temperature of space between galaxies
items.e: Particles have minimum kinetic energy.

items.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2,00 kg of lead (c = 130 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 40 K?
A gas absorbs 900 J of heat and does 350 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
items.e: First law: ΔU = Q − W = 550 J.

items.q: How does heat spread through the air in a room from a heater?
c: convection: warm air rises and cooler air sinks
items.e: Fluids carry energy as they move.

items.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1,50 kg of lead (c = 130 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 5 K?
items.e: Q = mcΔθ = 975 J.

items.q: When are two objects in thermal equilibrium?
c: when they have the same mass
when they have the same internal energy
when they are at the same temperature, so there is no net heat flow
items.e: This is the basis of the zeroth law.

items.q: A gas absorbs 1 300 J of heat and does 1 150 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
items.e: First law: ΔU = Q − W = 150 J.

items.q: A gas absorbs 1 500 J of heat and does 350 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
items.e: First law: ΔU = Q − W = 1 150 J.

items.q: Which change of state releases energy to the surroundings?
items.e: Steam burns are severe because of this.

items.q: What is the first law of thermodynamics?
c: heat always flows from cold to hot
the change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system (ΔU = Q − W)
energy is lost in every change
temperature can never reach absolute zero
items.e: It is conservation of energy.

items.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 0,800 kg of oil (c = 2 000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K?
A gas absorbs 1 100 J of heat and does 150 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
items.e: First law: ΔU = Q − W = 950 J.

items.q: What is temperature a measure of?
c: the potential energy of the particles
the amount of heat in an object
the total energy of the particles
the average kinetic energy of the particles
items.e: Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy.

items.q: A gas absorbs 1 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
items.e: First law: ΔU = Q − W = 1 300 J.

items.q: How does energy from the Sun reach Earth?
c: radiation (electromagnetic waves), which needs no medium
items.e: Space is a vacuum.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) or iodine (I<sub>2</sub>)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; iodine is larger (254 g/mol vs 160 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), hexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>), methane (CH<sub>4</sub>).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.
